sources.name: Alcohol Research Group / Public Health Institute, Alcohol Consumption Norms for U.S. Adults (2020 National Alcohol Survey)
sources.measures: Self-reported usual number of standard drinks per week over the past 12 months, as a cumulative distribution of all US adults including past-year abstainers (0 drinks). Rounded to the nearest percentile.
sources.notes: Cumulative shares for the total: 0 drinks (abstainers) 28%, 1 drink 58%, 10 drinks 87%, 12 drinks 89%, 13 drinks 89%, 14 drinks 90%, 15 drinks 91%, 16-17 drinks 92%, 18-19 drinks 93%, 50-59 drinks 98%, 60-69 drinks 99%, 70+ drinks 99%. The 99th percentile falls in the 60-69 drinks per week bin; no single value is published for it. Men: p50 is 1, p90 falls in the 18-19 bin (91%), p99 falls in the 70+ bin. Women: p50 is 0-1 (65% at 1), p90 is 10, p99 falls in 43-49. The ARG web page text gives 38% abstainers for women, but the table shows 31%. Funded by NIAAA grant P50AA005595.

sources.name: Alcohol Research Group, US drinking norms (2015 National Alcohol Survey, fielded 2014-15)
sources.measures: Self-reported usual number of drinks per week over the past 12 months, as a cumulative distribution of all US adults including past-year abstainers. Same table format and survey series as the 2020 norms.
sources.notes: Cumulative shares for the total: 0 drinks 33%, 1 drink 61%, 10 drinks 89%, 11 drinks 90%, 16-17 drinks 93%, 50-59 drinks 99%, 60-69 drinks 99%, 70+ drinks 100%. The 99th percentile falls in the 50-59 drinks per week bin. This is an independent sample from the 2020 wave, but the publisher and methods are the same.

definition: Self-reported usual number of standard drinks per week over the past 12 months, as a cumulative distribution of all US adults including past-year abstainers (0 drinks). Rounded to the nearest percentile.
caveat: The question asks about the top 10% of drinkers, but both sources rank all US adults, including the 28% (2020) to 33% (2015) who did not drink in the past year. So the p90 of 14 drinks a week (2020) is the cutoff for the top 10% of all adults. Restricting to drinkers would push the cutoff higher. In the 2020 table, the top 10% of drinkers is roughly the top 7% of all adults, which lands in the 18-19 drinks per week bin. That figure is read from the table, not published by ARG. Both sources are self-reported, and self-reports in US surveys cover only about half of alcohol sales, so true consumption is likely higher. The widely quoted figure that the top 10% of Americans average 74 drinks a week comes from Philip J. Cook's 'Paying the Tab' (2007). It uses NESARC 2001-02 data with each respondent's self-reported drinks multiplied by 1.97 to match sales. It is the mean within the top decile of adults, not a cutoff, so it measures something different and is not listed as a source. Cook's ninth decile averages about 15.3 drinks a week (as reported secondhand by Inc.). For comparison, NIAAA defines heavy drinking as more than 14 drinks a week for men and more than 7 for women. NCHS reported that 5.1% of US adults met the NHIS heavy-drinking definition in 2018.

new_metric.label: Alcoholic drinks per week
new_metric.definition: The usual number of standard alcoholic drinks a person consumes per week, self-reported over the past 12 months, with non-drinkers counted as zero.
